title: Give a Dog a Good Name
hook: Tell a man he is already careful with his things, within his hearing, and watch him spend the week proving you right.
counterintuition: Most people try to fix behavior by naming what is wrong with it, expecting the person to close the gap. The opposite move works better: name the better trait the person almost has, out loud, and let them quietly rearrange themselves to fit the name you gave them.
keyTakeaway: Pick a flattering trait the person almost has, name it aloud where they can hear, and they will quietly close the small gap to match the better picture you handed them.

breakdown.fastRead:
A boss tells the kid at the next desk, loud enough for the floor to hear, that he is the most reliable man on the team. The kid is not. Not yet. By Friday he is in early, checking his own work, walking toward the name his boss handed him.

That is the whole move. Give a person a good name to grow into, and most of them try.

People rise toward the version of themselves you say out loud, faster than they will ever rise toward a list of corrections. Nobody wakes up hoping to be straightened out before lunch.

Name the better person they almost are, say it where they can hear, and step out of their way.
breakdown.deepRead:
A second-chair cellist slides in late again as the warm-up ends. The conductor does not sigh. He waits until the visiting soloist arrives that afternoon and says, in the cellist's hearing, "This is our most reliable opener." Her face does something small. The next Tuesday she is in her chair ten minutes early.

Nothing was corrected. Nobody was scolded. A name was placed on her, and she walked toward it.

Why does this work when nagging does not? People defend their own picture of themselves the way they bolt a front door. Tell a woman she is sloppy and the lock slides shut, even when the charge is fair. Hand her a flattering description that is almost true, and there is no door to lock. There is only a small gap to close, and closing it is easier than calling you a liar.

The whole thing sits on the word almost. You cannot invent a quality out of thin air. The cellist had, somewhere, the seed of being reliable: one rehearsal she nailed, one solo she did not flub. Find that seed and name it.

Try it on the snapping checkout clerk. You watched her one Tuesday, gentle with an older woman counting pennies. That is your seed. Slip her a note that says the older shoppers are starting to ask for her line. Skip the lecture about the other days. Hand her the better version and walk on.

Pick one true thing, say it where she can hear it, and let her rise.
breakdown.fullRead:
A father pours coffee for his brother at the kitchen table. The eleven-year-old is in the next room, half listening, the way boys do. The father says, low and matter of fact, "He's getting careful about his things lately. Found his cleats in the right bin yesterday." That is all. The uncle nods. The talk moves on.

The boy, who has not in fact been careful, hears it. Something in him registers. By Saturday his cleats are in the bin again. By the next week his books. Nobody has yelled. Nobody has made a chart. A name has been placed on him, quietly, where he could overhear it, and he has begun walking toward it.

This is the oldest move in the parent's playbook, and the manager's, and the husband's, and most of us have forgotten it. Name the better trait a person almost has, and let them rise to meet the name.

The head nurse on a cardiac ward knows this. Her newest charge nurse is sloppy on medication checks, and on a cardiac ward sloppy means somebody's mother gets the wrong dose. Three write-ups in, the woman is days from quitting or being fired. The head nurse tries one more thing. Before the next shift, where two other nurses can hear, she says, "She is the most careful documenter we have had in years. You should see her handoff notes." It is barely true. One shift last Thursday the notes were clean. That much is enough. The young nurse hears it. By the end of the month the documentation is, in fact, the best on the floor. Not because anyone corrected her. Because someone handed her a name worth keeping.

Why does it work? Nearly everyone carries two pictures of themselves: the person they are on a bad day, and the person they would be if things were going right. Criticism forces them to defend the bad-day picture, because defending it feels like survival. Praise of the good-day picture, said as if it were already true, leaves them nothing to fight. There is only the distance between the name and the truth, and closing that distance is easier than being exposed as a fraud.

The rule has edges. The name must be almost true. Tell the chronically late hire she is the most punctual in the office and she will laugh in your face. Tell her you noticed she opened up clean on Monday, and you have handed her something real to grow into. Pick the smallest true fact and build the name on it.

The other edge is timing. Say it before any correction, not after. A name placed after a scolding sounds like a bandage. Said first, with no agenda showing, it lands as a description of who the person already is. The husband who overhears his wife tell her sister that he has been patient lately will spend the next month being quietly more patient, and the two of them will never have to sit down for the talk.

Find the one true thing about the better person they almost are, say it where they can hear it, and step back. Most of them will walk toward the name they have been given. The ones who will not were never going to be moved by a lecture anyway.

examples.title: Ingvar names the new charge nurse careful before her shift

planSpec.domain: a head nurse on a cardiac ward describing a sloppy new charge nurse to her face as 'the most careful documenter we've had in years' before the next shift
planSpec.audience: a charge nurse two years into management who keeps losing staff she has corrected
planSpec.stakes: whether the new hire stops cutting corners on med reconciliation or quits within the month after another write-up
planSpec.requiredBeat: the head nurse picks one true sliver of carefulness already visible in the new hire and names her by it before any correction lands, and the new hire is shown adjusting her own behavior to fit the name

examples.scenario: Ingvar, head nurse on the cardiac ward, watches the new charge nurse, Brigitta, hand off at 6:58 a.m. Brigitta has been sloppy with med reconciliation all week and a write-up is already drafted. But last Tuesday Brigitta caught a duplicate heparin order nobody else flagged. As the night team gathers, Ingvar says, loud enough for Brigitta to hear, 'Brigitta is the most careful documenter we've had in years. Watch how she logs the heparin holds.' Brigitta's pen, halfway to her pocket, stops. She sits back down and opens the chart again.
examples.whatToDo: Pick one true sliver of carefulness she has already shown, name her by it in front of her peers, and let the correction wait until she has tried on the name.
examples.whyItMatters: People defend the self-image already on file. Hand them a flattering one that is partly true, and they spend their effort earning it instead of fighting you for the old one.

examples.title: Ms. Pendergast names Constanza in the soloist's hearing

planSpec.domain: a high school orchestra conductor introducing a chronically late second-chair cellist to a visiting guest soloist
planSpec.audience: a music teacher at a public school with no leverage beyond words
planSpec.stakes: whether the cellist starts arriving at warm-up or the section drifts further out of tune for the spring concert
planSpec.requiredBeat: the conductor introduces the cellist by a reputation she has not yet earned ('our most reliable opener') in the soloist's hearing, and the cellist's face shifts as she registers the name being placed on her

examples.scenario: Ms. Pendergast spots the visiting soloist, Mr. Beltran, in the doorway of the band room just as Constanza shoves through the side door, ten minutes late, hair still wet from the rain. 'Maestro, come meet Constanza,' Ms. Pendergast says, steering him over. 'She's our most reliable opener. Has the section tuned before the rest of us put our coffee down.' Mr. Beltran nods, pleased. Constanza's mouth opens. It closes. She sets down her case, sits, and pulls out her tuning fork without a word.
examples.whatToDo: Introduce her in the soloist's hearing by the small virtue she could grow into, then walk away before she can argue it. Let the name she just heard become the deal she keeps with herself.
examples.whyItMatters: A reputation handed to someone in front of a witness she respects becomes a quiet debt she pays back in behavior. Correction asks her to defend her old self. A name lets her start being a new one.

examples.title: Atticus Names His Son Careful While Pouring His Brother's Coffee

planSpec.domain: a father at the kitchen table speaking about his eleven-year-old son's messy room within the son's hearing while pouring coffee for a visiting uncle
planSpec.audience: a parent of a preteen who has tried nagging and lost
planSpec.stakes: whether the boy starts picking up after himself without a fight, or the family settles into another year of weekend yelling
planSpec.requiredBeat: the father refers to the boy, casually and without performance, as someone who is becoming careful about his own things, and the boy overhears it and the room records what he does next without telling us what to feel

examples.scenario: Atticus pours coffee for his brother at the kitchen table. Down the hall, his son Jasper's door is half open, the floor still littered with hoodies and a cracked retainer case. Atticus does not lower his voice. 'Jasper's been getting careful about his good things lately. Folded that jersey his grandfather gave him without anyone asking.' He slides the sugar across. The footsteps in the hall pause, then start again, slower. A drawer opens. The hoodie draped on the chair by his door is gone before the uncle leaves.
examples.whatToDo: Within the boy's hearing, name him by the better trait he is almost showing, citing one true small instance. Do not announce it to him. Do not follow up. Let the name find him.
examples.whyItMatters: A child given a quiet reputation to live up to can reach for it without surrendering. Nagging asks him to admit you were right; an overheard description hands him a role he gets to grow into on his own terms.

examples.title: Wilbur Rewrites the Note to Doreen at Register Six

planSpec.domain: a regional grocery manager writing a one-paragraph note to a checkout clerk known for snapping at customers
planSpec.audience: a manager of forty hourly employees who cannot afford to fire the clerk
planSpec.stakes: whether the clerk's Saturday shift produces another customer complaint or whether her line becomes the one regulars choose
planSpec.requiredBeat: the before note is the corrective version the manager almost sent; the after is the version that names the clerk as 'the one our older shoppers ask for' on the strength of one true Tuesday interaction, and we see what arrives in his inbox a week later

examples.scenario: Wilbur runs four stores in the river district and has known Doreen at register six for nine years. Tuesday a customer wrote in: Doreen had carried her bag of cat litter to the parking lot in the rain. Wilbur's first draft reads, 'Doreen, the snapping at customers has to stop. Final warning.' He saves it to drafts. He starts over. The second note begins, 'Doreen, you are the one our older shoppers ask for. Mrs. Coyle wrote in about Tuesday.' He clips it to her schedule. A week later his inbox holds two notes from regulars asking when Doreen works.
examples.whatToDo: Throw out the corrective draft. Find the one true Tuesday moment that already shows the trait you want more of, and name her by it in a single sentence she will keep.
examples.whyItMatters: People rise toward the name placed on them. A reputation she has not quite earned becomes a target she can hit, while a corrective note becomes a verdict she spends the week defending against.

examples.title: Isadora at the lectern, choosing what to call her client

planSpec.domain: a public defender preparing a teenage client for a sentencing hearing where the judge has already read the file
planSpec.audience: a lawyer who knows the judge will be looking for a reason to be lenient or harsh
planSpec.stakes: whether the boy walks out with probation or with eighteen months in a youth facility
planSpec.requiredBeat: the lawyer must choose between defending the client against the file's worst readings or standing up and naming the client by a quality the judge has not yet seen evidence of, and the lawyer commits to the second move knowing the client will hear himself described that way for the first time

examples.scenario: Isadora has the file open on the lectern. Three pages of incidents, two suspensions, one fight in a parking lot. The judge has read all of it and is waiting. Her client, sixteen, sits behind her in a borrowed shirt that does not fit at the collar. She has ninety seconds of remarks before sentencing. She can spend them arguing the file down, page by page, or she can stand up and tell the judge that the boy behind her is the one in his family who keeps showing up. Both are partly true. She has to pick one in the next breath, knowing the boy will hear whichever she chooses.
examples.whatToDo: Stand up and name him by the quality you want the judge to look for. Say it plainly, in his hearing, then sit down before the room can argue with the name.
examples.whyItMatters: The judge is searching the room for a person, not a file. A name placed on the boy gives the judge somewhere to land leniency, and gives the boy a self to grow into on the way out the courthouse door.

examples.title: Genevieve Notices What She Named Her Husband

planSpec.domain: a long-married woman writing in her journal about how her husband answers the phone now compared to a year ago
planSpec.audience: a spouse trying to repair a marriage without sitting her partner down for a 'talk'
planSpec.stakes: whether the daily texture of the marriage softens or the couple drifts into separate rooms permanently
planSpec.requiredBeat: the woman traces back to one specific evening she described her husband to her sister as patient, in his hearing, and she notices on the page that he has been quietly trying to be that man ever since, without either of them naming the deal

examples.scenario: Genevieve sits at the kitchen table at half past ten, her tea cold, the journal open. She is trying to remember when her husband stopped sighing into the phone. She traces it back to a Sunday last year, her sister at the sink with her, him answering a contractor's call in the next room. She had said, plain as pouring water, 'He is the patient one of us, you know.' He heard her. She is sure of it now. He has been working at being that man ever since, and neither of them has ever said so out loud.
examples.whatToDo: Find one true, generous word for your spouse and use it about him in his hearing, then let him try to live up to it without ever telling him you noticed.
examples.whyItMatters: A name spoken to a third party lands harder than any direct compliment, because it sounds like a private verdict the speaker did not know was being overheard.

questions.prompt: A new café owner has read about giving employees 'a good name' and is sketching how she will use it with her three baristas this Monday. Which description captures the move most accurately?
choices: Find a trait the person already shows in full and praise them loudly for it whenever they display it.
Invent a flattering label about the person and use it consistently until repetition makes them grow into it.
Name a slightly better version of who the person almost is, anchored in one true sliver of evidence, so they have a name to live up to.
questions.explanation: The move points just ahead of where the person already is, anchored in something real so the label is not flattery. Praising a trait already in full does not pull anyone forward, and inventing a label with no evidence reads as manipulation and breaks trust.

questions.prompt: A youth soccer coach has a forward who keeps shooting from impossible angles instead of passing. The team is losing close games. A guest scout is watching practice tomorrow. What is the soundest move?
choices: After practice, walk her through the three games where she failed to pass and ask her to commit to changing.
In the huddle, with the scout listening, name her as the unselfish playmaker the squad is becoming, then run a passing drill.
Bench her for the first half of the next game so she feels the cost of her selfishness.
questions.explanation: Naming her as the unselfish playmaker, in the scout's hearing, hands her a reputation worth deserving in the next drill. Listing her failures fixes her self-image as a ball hog, and benching teaches resentment rather than the instinct to pass.

questions.prompt: A tech lead notices that a junior developer keeps merging code without writing tests. The lead wants to apply the 'name the better trait' approach. What works best?
choices: Configure the repository to block any merge that lowers test coverage and let the tooling do the correcting.
Send her a private message reminding her that test coverage is required and that she has been falling short.
At standup, mention that she is becoming the teammate others trust to leave the codebase safer than she found it, and ask her to demo her coverage on Friday.
questions.explanation: The standup mention names her as the careful teammate and the Friday demo gives her a stage to deserve the name. A merge block treats her as a problem to route around, and a private warning makes her cautious rather than proud of leaving good work behind.

questions.prompt: A library volunteer coordinator has a retired man who is reliable but speaks brusquely to the kids in the children's section. Several parents have noticed. What is the soundest move?
choices: Introduce him to the Friday story-time crew as the volunteer the youngest readers warm up to fastest, then ask him to greet them at the door.
Quietly reassign him to the back stacks where he will not interact with families.
Sit him down with the parent complaints and ask him to soften his tone going forward.
questions.explanation: Naming him as the volunteer kids warm up to gives him a part to play the next time a child approaches the desk. Reassigning him to the stacks punishes without teaching the warmth, and reading him the complaints puts him on the defensive before he has tried.

questions.prompt: A construction foreman has an apprentice carpenter who leaves tools scattered across the site at the end of every shift. The crew is fed up. What is the soundest move?
choices: While the site supervisor is visiting, mention that the apprentice is shaping up to be the most organized hand on the crew, citing how cleanly he staged yesterday's framing.
Dock his pay for the time the crew loses searching for tools at the end of each shift.
Pull him aside in front of two senior carpenters and tell him plainly that he is the messiest worker on the crew.
questions.explanation: Naming him as the most organized hand, in the supervisor's hearing and tied to one real Tuesday, gives him a reputation he will quietly work to deserve. Docking pay sparks resentment, and shaming him in front of seniors fixes 'the messy one' as his identity on the crew.

questions.prompt: A principal told a chronically tardy teacher at a staff meeting that he expects her to 'finally show some professionalism.' Six weeks later her arrival times are worse. What is the deepest reason the move backfired?
choices: Public correction in education settings is always less effective than a private one-on-one meeting.
He named her by the trait she was failing at rather than one she could rise to meet, so the label confirmed who she already was instead of pointing somewhere to grow.
She does not respect his authority and would have ignored any feedback he gave.
questions.explanation: A name only works as a pull when it points just past where the person already stands. 'Finally show some professionalism' reads as a verdict on her current self with nowhere to climb, while 'becoming the most reliable opener of the morning' would have given her somewhere to walk. Authority and venue are downstream of that.

questions.prompt: A regional manager praised a salesperson as 'one of the top closers in the territory' during the Monday huddle, when in fact she ranks near the bottom. She left visibly resentful. What is the issue?
choices: The named trait must already exist as one true sliver of evidence, however small. An unearned name reads as flattery, and the trust the move depends on collapses on contact with the leaderboard.
She is too cynical to respond to any kind of praise from leadership at this stage of her career.
Praise should never include comparisons to other employees because it always creates internal competition.
questions.explanation: Naming a trait works only when one honest example backs it up. Calling her a top closer when the leaderboard says otherwise insults her intelligence and burns the move for next time. Cynicism and comparison rules are not the cause: an honest reference to one strong call would have landed.

questions.prompt: A swim coach told a struggling distance swimmer she was 'becoming an elite-level competitor' right after she finished last at a regional meet. She rolled her eyes and skipped the next two practices. Why did the move fail?
choices: Athletes that age reject all coach praise as a developmental phase, and the timing did not really matter.
He should have benched her from the next meet so she would understand the seriousness of her finish.
Said in the moment of the loss, the naming read as consolation for finishing last rather than recognition of something already real, like a strong split or a clean turn she could be proud of.
questions.explanation: A name placed on top of a fresh failure gets heard as a pep talk to soften the blow. The move requires pointing at a real sliver, like one strong 100 in the middle of the race, so the swimmer can recognize herself in the description. Benching teaches shame; the rejection theory excuses the coach.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit director has a board member who chronically misses meetings but brings strong donor connections. Which option is the soundest application of the principle?
choices: Send the full board the attendance roster with chronic absences highlighted in red so the social pressure does the work.
At the next gala, in the board member's hearing, mention that she has become the most dependable connector the board has, citing the introduction she made in March.
Stop inviting her to working sessions entirely and quietly use her only as a name on the donor solicitation list.
questions.explanation: Naming her as the most dependable connector at the gala, anchored in one real introduction, gives her a reputation to deserve at the next meeting. The highlighted roster shames her without offering a way up, and quietly sidelining her writes her off and forfeits the chance to change anything.

reviewCards.front: You need someone to change a habit you find sloppy. Before you correct them, what is the move this principle asks for?
reviewCards.back: Name the better trait the person almost has, then let them rise to meet the name you gave them. Find one true sliver of the quality you want more of, say it plainly within their hearing, and let the name do the pulling instead of the rebuke.

reviewCards.front: A checkout clerk on your team snaps at customers, but on Tuesday you watched her walk an older shopper to aisle nine. You sit down to write her a note. What goes on the page?
reviewCards.back: Skip the corrective draft. Write the version that names her as the clerk your older shoppers ask for, on the strength of that Tuesday walk. The accurate seed of praise gives her a reputation she will quietly start protecting, which the warning never would.

reviewCards.front: Your eleven year old will not pick up his room and nagging has stopped working. A relative is coming over for coffee. How do you use the visit?
reviewCards.back: While pouring coffee, mention to the relative, casually and without performance, that the boy is becoming careful about his own things. Let him overhear it and do not follow up. You have placed a name on him that he can now grow into without losing face to you.

reviewCards.front: You are defending a teenager at sentencing. The judge has read a file full of the boy's worst moments. You can rebut the file or you can do something else. What is the harder, better move, and why does it work even on a judge?
reviewCards.back: Stand up and name the client by a quality the file has not shown yet, in language the boy himself will hear for the first time. The judge gets a reputation to test against the sentence she is about to hand down, and the boy gets a name to start trying to deserve. Defending line by line only argues inside the file's frame.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You are practicing the skill of naming the better version of someone before they have fully earned the name, then trusting them to grow into it. It is a small act of public faith that costs you nothing and gives the other person a self-image worth defending. Done well, it replaces the hours you used to spend correcting with one true sentence said in front of a witness.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you are about to write a corrective note to someone on your team, then first find one real moment from the last two weeks where they showed the trait you wish they had more of, and open the note by naming them as the kind of person who does that.

If you catch yourself about to remind your partner of a habit you wish they would change, then instead, in earshot of a friend or family member, mention the version of that habit they already do well and stop talking.
If your child or younger sibling overhears you on the phone, then describe them to the person on the other end by the trait you most want them to grow into, and let them hear it without comment.

If you are introducing a volunteer or a new neighbor to a third person, then introduce them by the contribution you hope they will make, not the one already on their resume, and watch what they do next.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, pick one person you have been quietly disappointed in and write down one true sliver of the better trait you wish they had more of. Tomorrow, in front of at least one other person, refer to them by that trait, in a single plain sentence, and then change the subject.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, on the same day, look at the three people whose behavior is costing you the most patience. For each one, write down the name you would like to give them, the small true evidence that backs it up, and the witness you will say it in front of. Spend the rest of the week saying those names out loud where they can hear, and keep notes on what shifts.

memorableLines.text: Tell a man he is already careful with his things, within his hearing, and watch him spend the week proving you right.
memorableLines.why: Demonstrates the mechanic in concrete, specific language with an immediate visible result that shows the principle working in real time.

memorableLines.text: Nobody wakes up hoping to be straightened out before lunch.
memorableLines.why: A humanizing observation that captures why correction fails, voiced with unexpected humor and grounded in the reader's own experience.

memorableLines.text: There is only the distance between the name and the truth, and closing that distance is easier than being exposed as a fraud.
memorableLines.why: Reveals the hidden psychology that makes the technique work—the reader realizes people choose self-improvement over admitting you were right about them.
